population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. About 66M of ~268M US adults are currently on an incretin for any indication (0.246×268 ≈ 66M). Age check: 0.20×14 + 0.33×25 + 0.24×37 + 0.23×20 ≈ 24.5. Income thirds (19/25/30) average 24.7. Most of the bottom third's gain from 12% to 19% comes from $60–110 gray-market imports and $149 TrumpRx orals, not from insurance. Cycling: ever 31.5% − current 24.6% = 6.9 pp of adults (~18.5M) have used and are off now. With the 2029 Wegovy recall and Medicare lockouts adding churn, about 38% of current users are restarters (0.38×24.6 ≈ 9.3 pp), and about 25% of those currently off had cycled before (0.25×6.9 ≈ 1.7 pp), so (9.3+1.7)/31.5 ≈ 35% of ever-users have stopped and restarted at least once. Payer mix of the 66M current users: diabetes-, cardiac-, renal-, OSA- or MASH-coded coverage across all payers ~23M; employer obesity coverage ~6.5M (down from 8M); Medicare Continuity Model ~2.0M; Medicaid adult obesity (same 19 states) ~1.9M; brand cash via TrumpRx/direct ~17M; gray market ~15.6M. These sum to 66.0M. Off-drug population: ~18.5M former users. Of those, ~6.5M stopped for coverage or supply reasons, including ~210k Medicare beneficiaries locked out after recall-driven refill gaps in 2029. Among adults with BMI ≥30 who have never used the drug, cost is still the most cited reason, ahead of preference. Pediatric: ~1.4% of under-18s (~1.0M), of whom ~120k are aged 6–11, mostly on generic liraglutide since the Nov 2029 approval. Medicaid/CHIP covers under-12 use through existing EPSDT medical-necessity rules; affluent families pay cash for adolescent semaglutide. Roughly one child in three lives in a household where an adult is on the drug.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the CMS GLP-1 Continuity Model is unchanged at $245/month paid and ~$50 copay, with the ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered rule, the ≥5% loss at 6 months rule and the 12-month lockout. About 2.0M obesity-only beneficiaries are enrolled. Spending: 2.0M × $245 × 12 ≈ $5.9B/yr, running above CBO's ~$4B/yr path. About 210k beneficiaries were locked out in 2029 after the Wegovy pen recall caused refill gaps. CMS issued no exception, and a class action over those lockouts is pending. MariTide is not yet in the model. Medicaid: the same 19 states cover adult obesity at $245 for ~1.9M adults. Gross cost 1.9M × $245 × 12 ≈ $5.6B/yr; federal share at ~65% FMAP ≈ $3.6B. Children aged 6–17 are covered in all states under EPSDT once a labelled indication exists, mainly with generic liraglutide.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India has 70+ generic semaglutide brands, injectable and oral, at ~$8–40/month. Chinese generic semaglutide (post-2026 patent expiry) is now exported at scale to Southeast Asia, Latin America and the Gulf. Canada, Brazil, Mexico and Turkey have generics at roughly CAD 60–100 or local equivalents. Generic liraglutide is available in the US. US semaglutide and tirzepatide exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32.
access.note: The price shock comes from supply. The Feb 2029 Wegovy pen recall and fill-finish shutdown pushed Novo's direct injectable semaglutide price from $199 to $279; it had eased to $249 by late 2030. Lilly raised top-dose Zepbound vials from $299 to $349 as Wegovy users switched. Zepbound now costs $249–349, retatrutide stays at $399 direct, and MariTide launched at $449/month direct cash (list ~$1,450). Orals were unaffected: they are small-molecule or tablet supply chains, and TrumpRx initial doses stay at $149. About 55% of new starts are now oral. Employer weight-management coverage fell 44% → 40% (2029) → 36% (2030, Business Group on Health). Nearly all of the remainder requires a T2D, CVD, CKD, OSA or MASH code, or BMI ≥35 with comorbidity plus enrolment in a vendor programme. Gray market: during the Feb–Oct 2029 shortage listing, 503A and 503B compounders could lawfully copy semaglutide again, and the product stayed in circulation after the listing ended. Personal-importation telehealth (Indian and Chinese generics at $60–110) is the largest gray channel. Counterfeit branded pens sold through social-media resellers are a smaller but deadlier channel. In total ~15.6M users (~24%).

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda and generics; now labelled 6+)
GLP-1 agonist / GIPR antagonist antibody conjugate, monthly injectable (maridebart cafraglutide: MariTide, Amgen; approved May 2030)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: smoking and nicotine-vaping cessation in adults with overweight or obesity (semaglutide, 2028)
alcohol use disorder in adults (semaglutide, Mar 2030)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: gambling and sports-betting compulsion, prescribed by telehealth since the 2029 phase 3 readouts (sNDA filed Sep 2030)
compulsive shopping and 'screen compulsion', via the same telehealth services
semaglutide in children 6–11 (pending the STEP Young sNDA)
drugs.pipeline_note: MariTide: Amgen filed Feb 2029, approved May 2030 (15 months after filing), launched Jul 2030. It gives ~17–20% loss at 72 weeks with monthly dosing. The first-dose GI burden is mitigated by step-up dosing. It satisfies the 'monthly' driver, and many employers' vendor programmes favour clinic administration. No implant exists on the US market; implant programmes are preclinical or phase 1. Amycretin: filed Q2 2029, under FDA review, decision expected 2031. Survodutide: filed Q1 2029, approved Sep 2030 for obesity with MASH; launch is 2031. 'Compulsion' driver: the AUD approval (Mar 2030) is the first approved compulsive-use indication. It came from the phase 3 that read out in 2029. A gambling-disorder sNDA for semaglutide was filed Sep 2030 on two RCTs (one Danish, one US), with priority review and a decision due 2031. Gambling use is therefore off-label and widespread, not approved. The pediatric under-12 driver is realised through liraglutide (SCALE Kids); semaglutide's STEP Young sNDA is under review. The global incretin market is ~$150B (2030).

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Worst with retatrutide top doses, MariTide's first monthly dose and uncontrolled gray-market titration.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MariTide label requires step-up initiation.

safety_ledger.effect: Gastroparesis, ileus and bowel obstruction (mass-tort scale)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Delayed gastric emptying is a known mechanism. Severe or persistent gastroparesis after discontinuation is disputed. MDL 3094 (E.D. Pa.) grew from ~3,000 to ~38,000 claims by late 2030, driven by plaintiff advertising. Under the court's earlier rulings, gastroparesis claims need a gastric-emptying study. Several thousand claims involve compounded or counterfeit product, which complicates attribution.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Ileus labelled class-wide. First bellwether verdict Oct 2030: $11.5M for the plaintiff on failure-to-warn over ileus, under appeal. Novo and Lilly disclose combined litigation reserves of ~$2.4B.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid loss; higher in real-world retatrutide use.
No causal confirmation in long RCTs and absolute risk stays low. Now joined to the MDL; pancreatic cancer claims were mostly dismissed on general causation in 2029.
The bone-density association in women over 60 was replicated in a 2029 US cohort. Muscle preservation depends on trainers and protein budgets, so it is unevenly distributed by income.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Retatrutide and MariTide labels recommend resistance exercise; no class warning.
EMA 'very rare' label; no US class label.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The AUD and cessation trials showed no excess.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning stays removed from US labels.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The AUD phase 3 was the first to include the validated SHAPS anhedonia scale, added after advocacy pressure. Clinically meaningful anhedonia appeared in ~3% on drug vs ~1% on placebo, mostly reversible on dose reduction. It is uncommon, but at 66M users that is roughly 1–1.5M people if the rate generalises. Prevalence outside trial populations is unmeasured.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Since Mar 2030, 'anhedonia/apathy (uncommon)' appears in the semaglutide adverse-reactions section, and MariTide carries similar wording. There is no boxed warning. Some telehealth services now use a two-question screen at refill.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The 2029 recall caused the largest single wave of involuntary stops; roughly half of lost weight returns within a year.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. It still justifies the Medicare and Medicaid adherence rules.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: More reports in retatrutide users and in children; pediatric dietitian access is scarce in Medicaid networks.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Society guidance recommends baseline and annual labs.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; adolescents; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Interim Sentinel cycling analysis (2030) finds no excess cardiovascular events but greater gallbladder events per restart. Adolescents who started in 2023–25 begin crossing 5 years.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements; final Sentinel report due 2032.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FDA adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed ~14,000 by mid-2030. In the Sep–Nov 2029 CDC cluster, counterfeit 'Ozempic' pens filled with insulin caused ~190 ER visits for severe hypoglycaemia and 7 deaths in five states. Endotoxin and dosing-error reports continue from compounded and research-peptide product.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: CDC Health Alert; FDA import alerts widened to Chinese shippers; platform takedown agreements with Meta and TikTok. Personal importation is still largely unenforced.

safety_ledger.effect: Acquired olfactory and taste dysfunction after ≥5 years continuous use
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A US claims-plus-smell-test cohort (2029) found a hazard ratio of ~1.3, smaller than the Nordic study. Confounding by diabetes duration is partly addressed but not excluded.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA PRAC added 'smell disorder' to EU semaglutide labelling (2029). The FDA added it to postmarketing experience in Jan 2030 without a warning.

safety_ledger.effect: Growth, puberty and eating-behaviour effects in children 6–11
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: SCALE Kids ran 56 weeks, so effects on linear growth and pubertal timing over longer horizons are unknown. Pediatric dietitians report restrictive-eating presentations. No signal is quantified.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The liraglutide 6–11 label requires growth monitoring, and a 10-year registry is a postmarketing requirement.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~36% of US households. Snack and confectionery unit volumes are down ~6–7% from 2026 and sugary drinks ~5%. Companion lines and protein SKUs are mainstream, and private-label snack makers closed further Midwest plants (Iowa, Ohio). Retailers report the sharpest declines in affluent suburban stores; discount-grocer baskets in poorer counties have changed less.

alcohol.state: With the AUD approval, heavy-drinker decline is now a labelled indication. US spirits volumes are down a further ~5% over two years and beer ~3%. Distillers lobby against AUD direct-to-consumer advertising. Tobacco keeps 'incretin adoption' in its risk factors. Sportsbooks (DraftKings, FanDuel) added incretin compulsion prescribing to 10-K risk factors in 2030 after reporting lower handle among high-frequency bettors in early cohorts.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat to slightly down and average ticket is held by premium small plates. Half-portion menus are standard. Buffet closures continue. Protein-forward fast casual is the clearest winner. Bars in college towns are the soft spot.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep closing stores. Tailoring and 'athletic slim' cuts sell at a premium in affluent markets. Off-price chains carry more mid-size inventory from people who cycled. Return rates on fitted items rose again during the 2029 recall regain.

fitness.state: Strength studios, private trainers and 'muscle-insurance' memberships ($150–300/month) are growing fastest in affluent zip codes, often bundled with brand GLP-1 telehealth. Big-box gyms add free-weight floors. Gray-market peptides keep spreading through gym communities.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is down to 36%. Coverage concentrates on diabetes, cardiac, renal, sleep-apnea and liver codes. About 1 in 4 large self-funded employers attach a BMI or adherence surcharge. Wellness vendors increasingly favour MariTide's clinic-administered monthly dose, which verifies adherence directly. Pharmacy trend is ~7%.

pharma.state: Lilly is dominant and gained share from the Wegovy recall. Novo rebuilt fill-finish capacity at a cost of ~$1B in lost US sales in 2029. Amgen entered with MariTide. Litigation reserves are now material. Ex-US volume is dominated by Indian and Chinese generics.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Shape now reads as income. A lean body with visible muscle (in Highland Park, Dallas or Brookline, Massachusetts) says brand drug, trainer and protein budget. Lean without muscle, the 'import look' of fast gray-market loss in older adults, says cash-strapped. A larger body says no coverage, a lockout or refusal, and the default assumption has shifted toward the first two.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The tiers are explicit. On-drug rates are 30% in the top third and 19% in the bottom, but the gap that shows is in quality: brand versus import, trainer versus none, continuous versus cycled. Strength-studio memberships, ultra-processed-free groceries and MariTide's clinic visits have become markers of status. Hourly workers at large self-funded employers in Columbus, Ohio and the Inland Empire pay BMI surcharges, often while on an import that no wellness vendor recognises.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Half portions are the professional norm. In affluent households 'protein first' has turned into a coached ritual. Church potlucks and family reunions in the South and Midwest still split by table, and the off-drug table is increasingly a poorer table. Children on liraglutide bring smaller lunches, and school nurses in some districts keep lists.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: In big-city apps, muscle tone has replaced 'on it/off it' as the shorthand. 'Reta and rack' is a recognised profile type. Some clinics now ask couples about libido and apathy, and partners can name a labelled side effect where before they described a mood.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Every appetite with a market now has a molecule: food, nicotine, alcohol and, by telehealth, betting. The counter-movements persist. Atlanta and Oakland fat-liberation groups now frame the issue as class rather than identity ('your body is your pay stub'), which brings them closer to labour organisers. 'Made Whole' congregations in Texas and Oklahoma grow among people locked out of coverage.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: The SHAPS data in the AUD trial (~3% vs ~1%) put anhedonia/apathy on the label as uncommon. Clinicians now accept it as a minority effect, usually dose-responsive, and manage it by stepping down or switching drugs. Real-world prevalence is not measured. The trial population was people with AUD, and nobody knows whether the rate holds for weight users or for children.
interior_life.framing: It is called a side effect, a known and uncommon one that you report to your prescriber. The larger quieting of wanting is still framed as treatment, especially for drinking, smoking and betting.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Employers keep praising 'steady' staff. A few EAP providers added apathy to GLP-1 check-in scripts, and one sales-heavy software firm's internal memo telling reps they could 'discuss dose with your doctor before Q4' leaked and became a joke. No employer policy references the label.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Touring musicians talk openly about stepping down a dose before tours or recording. Bar trivia and bowling leagues keep thinning. Sports-bar betting nights in Midwest college towns are visibly quieter. High-sensation live formats keep growing.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples therapists now cite the label. Partners name 'apathy' as a reason for a dose change. Most people experiencing lower desire still attribute it to age or stress.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The label took some force out of the 'sedating the workforce' charge, since an uncommon side effect makes a weak conspiracy. The fight moved to gambling: sportsbook-friendly legislators and recovery advocates spar over whether off-label prescribing for betting should be advertised. There is no measurable effect on turnout.

state.regulatory_posture: Unchanged in structure. The FDA moves fast on approvals and indications: MariTide, survodutide, liraglutide 6–11 and semaglutide AUD. It acts against counterfeits through alerts and platform agreements but lacks staff for personal importation. It made no new rules this step. CMS kept the Continuity Model terms through the recall without granting an exception.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Price-controlled public access continues at $245, and the TrumpRx cash channel remains. Pediatric Medicaid coverage flows from existing EPSDT obligations, not from new law.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Medicare and the seven waiver Medicaid states still require ≥80% PDC and ≥5% loss at 6 months, with a 12-month lockout. About 1 in 4 large self-funded employers use BMI surcharges ($50–100/month), waived on biometric proof or on verified adherence via connected pen or clinic administration. Gray-market users cannot prove adherence to vendors, so the poorest drug users pay surcharges anyway. Texas's surcharge ban still exempts ERISA plans.
state.workforce_or_military: Army and Air Force accession waivers continue, requiring ≥6 months off-drug stability. Recruiters report more applicants who used import product without records. TRICARE terms are unchanged.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Novo's fill-finish failure exposed how few US sterile injectable lines exist. Lilly and Novo cite it in tariff talks to keep relief. Chinese generic exporters joined Indian ones as targets of FDA import alerts. Counterfeit pens trace to repackagers in several countries. Canadian generic semaglutide is still bought by border-state residents.

events.event: Novo Nordisk recalls 1.4 million Wegovy and Ozempic pens after sterility failures at a contract fill-finish site; FDA returns semaglutide injectables to the shortage list until October, compounders legally resume copies, Novo lifts its direct price from $199 to $279, and roughly 210,000 Medicare enrollees lose coverage when refill gaps break the 80% adherence rule.

CDC Health Alert: counterfeit 'Ozempic' pens containing insulin, sold through social-media resellers, tied to about 190 emergency visits for severe hypoglycaemia and seven deaths in Texas, Florida, Georgia, Arizona and Ohio; FDA counts some 11,000 adverse-event reports linked to unapproved incretins.

FDA approves liraglutide, including generic versions, for obesity in children aged 6 to 11, citing the SCALE Kids trial; state Medicaid programmes begin covering it under EPSDT rules, and a semaglutide application for the same age group goes under review.

FDA approves semaglutide for alcohol use disorder, the first label to list 'anhedonia/apathy' as an uncommon adverse reaction after the trial found it in about 3% of patients versus 1% on placebo; in September Novo files for gambling disorder, already a common off-label telehealth use.

FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first monthly obesity injection, 15 months after filing; it launches in July at $449 a month in cash, and several large wellness vendors say they will accept clinic-administered doses as proof of adherence.

A Philadelphia federal jury returns an $11.5 million verdict against Novo Nordisk in the first bellwether trial of the GLP-1 multidistrict litigation, over an ileus failure-to-warn claim; the MDL now holds about 38,000 gastroparesis, obstruction and pancreatitis claims.

open_tensions: Compulsion is turning into an indication. A gambling-disorder decision is due in 2031 while telehealth already prescribes for betting, shopping and screens. Sportsbooks, distillers and recovery advocates are fighting over it, and the only label measure of the cost is an anhedonia rate from one AUD trial that nobody has tested in weight users or children.

Mass-tort litigation is maturing just as use broadens. With ~38,000 claims and a first plaintiff verdict, reserves and label pressure are rising. Thousands of the claims involve counterfeit or compounded product, which blurs causation for courts and regulators alike.

Adherence surveillance now punishes supply failures. Medicare locked out ~210k people for gaps the manufacturer caused, a class action is pending, and MariTide's clinic dosing gives employers the verified-adherence data they wanted. Meanwhile the gray-market poor pay surcharges they cannot waive.

About 120k children aged 6–11 are on drug, concentrated in Medicaid and wealthy families, with growth data running to only 56 weeks. Their exposure clock started alongside the adolescent cohort's five-year mark and the 2031–32 US generic cliff, when price, and probably use, will move again.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US; brand exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32.
The TrumpRx cash channel still operates, with oral initial doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) at $149/month.

Medicare pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 beneficiary copay under the CMS GLP-1 Continuity Model, which still requires ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered, ≥5% loss at 6 months, and imposes a 12-month lockout on lapse.
Wegovy's list price is still $1,349/month, and almost nobody pays it.
Texas's 2027 ban on BMI-based premium surcharges still applies only to state-regulated plans; ERISA self-funded employers remain exempt.

prose.headline: 66 Million on the Drug, and Your Body Shows Which Tier Pays for It
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2030 a quarter of American adults, about 66 million people, are on an incretin drug. Another 18 million have been on one and stopped, and more than a third of everyone who has ever started has stopped and started again. The drug is now less a treatment than an economy, and its tiers can be seen on the street.

The tiers come from who pays. Codes still protect people with diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease or sleep apnea. Obesity alone is protected less every year: only 36 percent of employers still cover weight management, and most of those want a comorbidity and a vendor programme first. The middle class pays cash. A $149 daily pill is the cheapest door, and more than half of new patients now go through it. Below that is the import economy. Telehealth services ship Indian and now Chinese generic semaglutide for $60 to $110 a month under a personal-importation rule nobody enforces, and they serve nearly one user in four.

Prices went up because of a failure, not a policy. In February 2029 Novo Nordisk recalled 1.4 million pens after sterility failures at a fill-finish plant. Injectable semaglutide went back on the federal shortage list, compounders were legally allowed to copy it again, and Novo's direct price rose from $199 to $279. People switched to Lilly's drugs and to pills, and Lilly raised its top-dose price. In Medicare, the recall ran into the adherence rules built in 2028. About 210,000 beneficiaries whose pharmacies had no pens fell below the 80 percent refill threshold and were locked out for a year. CMS made no exception, and a class action is pending.

The shortage also fed the counterfeits. In autumn 2029 the CDC traced counterfeit Ozempic pens, filled with insulin and sold through social-media resellers, to about 190 emergency visits and seven deaths across five states. Since then pharmacists show customers how to read lot numbers, and telehealth importers advertise their batch certificates.

Body shape now reads as income. In Highland Park or Brookline, the look is lean with visible muscle: a brand drug, a trainer, a protein budget, sometimes the new monthly shot. Amgen's MariTide arrived in July at $449 a month, and wellness vendors like it because a nurse gives the dose and the data follows. The import look is thinner and softer, the face looser. A warehouse worker in Columbus may be on a drug and still pay the BMI surcharge, because a pen from Hyderabad doesn't sync to her employer's app.

The drug's reach into appetite widened. In March it was approved for alcohol use disorder, and the trial behind that approval was the first to measure anhedonia properly. About 3 percent of patients on the drug lost interest in things they had enjoyed, against 1 percent on placebo, and the label now says so. 'Ozempic personality' has become a line item, an uncommon side effect you mention to your doctor, which makes it harder to use as a political charge. Gambling is the next fight. Telehealth services already prescribe for sports betting, Novo filed for a gambling indication in September, and the sportsbooks have added the drug to their risk disclosures.

Children are part of it now. Liraglutide was approved for ages six to eleven in late 2029, and Medicaid covers it under existing obligations, so the youngest users are disproportionately poor children and rich ones. Their growth data covers 56 weeks.

The lawsuits have grown to match the market. A multidistrict court in Philadelphia holds about 38,000 claims of gastroparesis, obstruction and pancreatitis, and in October a jury returned the first plaintiff verdict, $11.5 million. Nothing has collapsed. Snacks and spirits are down a few more points, strength gyms are up, and the country looks healthier to anyone who doesn't ask who is paying for it.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Dana Kowalczyk clocks in at the Groveport distribution centre at 5:52 and stops at the wellness kiosk by the break room, because it is the first Tuesday. Shoes off, step up. The screen says BMI 30.4 and SURCHARGE CONTINUES: $75/MO. She has lost thirty-one pounds on the semaglutide she orders from a site with an Indian pharmacy's batch certificate in the footer, $89 a month. The kiosk doesn't know that. It wants a pen that syncs.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap and gives the other half to Luis, who isn't on anything and says he never will be, mostly because of the price. Her shift lead, Brandon, walks past in a fitted company quarter-zip. His forearms look like a trainer did them. His plan covers the monthly shot.

At three she texts her sister: did you check your lot number. Her sister sends back a photo of the box, and Dana compares it against the list the pharmacist at Kroger taped by the register after the insulin pens.

At home Mason, nine, is at the counter drawing a dragon. She takes the liraglutide pen out of the butter drawer, where Medicaid's supply lives, and he holds out his stomach without looking up. Nationwide Children's measures his height every three months. He has grown half an inch. He packs a smaller lunch than his friends do and has stopped asking for the cafeteria cookie.

After he's asleep she sits on the porch and can't remember the last time she wanted anything badly. Then she decides that is probably what being forty-four feels like.
